subject: Banking
title: How the Fed Is Structured
description: A micro-lesson that makes How the Fed Is Structured usable.

hook.text: The Fed isn't one bank. It's 12 regional reserve banks plus a Board of Governors in Washington.

buildup.text: The Board of Governors has 7 members appointed by the president.

discovery.text: The FOMC, which sets rates, has 12 voting members: all 7 governors plus 5 rotating reserve bank presidents.

twist.text: Regional reserve banks are technically private. Their boards include commercial bankers.

climax.text: The Fed is half public, half private, and entirely powerful.

punchline.text: 12 banks, 7 governors, one rate. The Fed was built on compromise.

quiz.question: How many regional reserve banks make up the Federal Reserve System?

details.summary: The Federal Reserve is a hybrid public-private institution with a Board of Governors in Washington, twelve regional Reserve Banks, and the Federal Open Market Committee that sets interest rate policy for the world's largest economy.
details.whyItMatters: The Fed's unique structure balances political accountability with operational independence. Understanding how it works is essential because its decisions on interest rates ripple through every economy on the planet.
takeaways: The Board of Governors has seven members appointed by the president
Twelve regional Reserve Banks represent different geographic districts
The FOMC has twelve voting members who set the federal funds rate

faq.question: Why does the Fed have twelve regional banks?
faq.answer: When the Fed was created in 1913, Congress wanted to distribute power away from Wall Street. The twelve regional banks ensure that economic conditions across the entire country, not just New York, inform monetary policy decisions.

faq.question: Who actually decides interest rates?
faq.answer: The Federal Open Market Committee votes on the federal funds rate target. The FOMC includes all seven Board Governors and five of twelve regional bank presidents on a rotating basis, with the New York Fed president as a permanent voting member.
